Beyond Words: Evaluating and Bridging Epistemic Divergence
in User-Agent Interaction via Theory of Mind

Minyuan Ruan Affiliation: Dept. of Comp. Sci. & Tech., Institute for AI, Tsinghua University, Beijing, China    Ziyue Wang Affiliation: Dept. of Comp. Abstract

Large Language Models (LLMs) have developed rapidly and are widely applied to both general-purpose and professional tasks to assist human users. However, they still struggle to comprehend and respond to the true user needs when intentions and instructions are imprecisely conveyed, leading to a divergence between subjective user believes and true environment states. Resolving this epistemic divergence requires Theory of Mind (ToM), yet existing ToM evaluations for LLMs primarily focus on isolated belief inference, overlooking its functional utility in real-world interaction. To this end, we formalize ToM for LLMs as a mechanism for epistemic divergence detection and resolution, and propose a benchmark, SynchToM, to assess how models reconcile user beliefs and profiles in practice. Results across 11 leading models reveal a significant limitation to identify underlying cognitive gaps that impede task success. To bridge this gap, we further curate a trajectory-based ToM dataset linking belief tracking with task-related state inference. The model trained on this data via reinforcement learning shows consistent improvement in reasoning about user mental states, leading to enhanced downstream performance. Our work highlights the practical value of ToM as an essential interaction-level mechanism rather than as a standalone reasoning skill. 11 1 Code and data will be available: https://github.com/THUNLP-MT/SynchToM.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

The rapid evolution of Large Language Models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents (Gao et al., 2025) has enabled them to accomplish a wide range of common and professional tasks, leading to their widespread application in diverse scenarios, such as coding (Yang et al., 2024), medical healthcare (Li et al., 2024) and GUI (Wang et al., 2025a). Despite these advances, a significant understanding gap persists, where models fail to explicitly capture and correctly respond to the true user intent (Chang et al., 2025). This failure frequently stems from a miscalibration of user beliefs and an insufficient grasp of the user cognitive background. While human interpretations of the world are inherently shaped by diverse backgrounds and cognitive profiles, individual beliefs often vary and may diverge from objective reality (Dardenne & Leyens, 1995; Boven et al., 2013).

This epistemic divergence between subjective beliefs and the objective world forms the fundamental premise of Theory of Mind (ToM) (Premack & Woodruff, 1978; Apperly, 2010). While such discrepancies hamper communication and may impede the effectiveness of the agentic assistance, ToM provides the necessary capacity to resolve them by ascribing mental states to others. Since perspectives of individuals naturally vary in social interactions, this ability to attribute mental states is a prerequisite for efficient communication and collaboration, as it helps one remain cognizant of potential divergences. With the proliferation of LLM agents (Yang et al., 2025b), a comparable capability is essential for fluent interaction (Yao et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2025). As shown in Figure 1, ToM requires the agent, who has access to world knowledge, to construct an accurate representation of user beliefs and profiles (Rabinowitz et al., 2018; Sun et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025), identify critical gaps between user beliefs and objective reality, and actively manage these discrepancies. By reconciling latent user beliefs with factual environment states, the agent can guide users toward correct resolutions and prevent the persistence of erroneous mental states.

Previous work primarily focuses on assessing whether LLMs exhibit human-level Theory of Mind (ToM) reasoning (Chen et al., 2024; Gandhi et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2024) and enhancing such capabilities through prompting strategies (Sclar et al., 2023; Wilf et al., 2024; Jung et al., 2024) or training-based approaches (Tang & Belle, 2024; Lu et al., 2025) that directly expose models to differences in individual perspectives. While these studies successfully locate shortcomings of LLMs in ToM reasoning literally, and improve the accuracy of static ToM benchmark with simplified environment, it remains controversial whether LLMs truly acquire ToM capabilities beyond passive question-answering (Riemer et al., 2025). Moreover, much of this work conceptualizes ToM as an isolated cognitive capability, without integrating it into practical, user-oriented interaction settings.

Building on these observations, we raise two Research Questions: RQ1: Can ToM be evaluated via its utility in practical scenarios rather than as an isolated cognitive task? RQ2: How can ToM-based reasoning be integrated to improve downstream task performance?

In this work, we formalize ToM for LLMs as a mechanism for epistemic divergence detection in practical interactions. Due to the inherent limitation of individuals operating from a first-person perspective as illustrated in Figure 1, we model the environment as a partially observable process, characterizing both users and agents as belief-driven actors with asymmetric access to information. On this basis, we design a pipeline to simulate this mechanism and curate a benchmark, SynchToM, to evaluate the practicality of ToM through belief calibration, profile modeling, and task resolution. Our evaluation indicates that current LLMs often struggle to identify the causes of erroneous user beliefs, which also leads to failures in resolution where models prioritize instruction-following over epistemic alignment. To bridge this gap, we enhance the practicality of ToM via reinforcement learning using interactive instances generated by our pipeline. Corresponding results highlight the importance of ToM in user-agent interaction and practical task-solving. Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We formalize ToM for LLMs as a functional mechanism for epistemic divergence detection, shifting focus from theoretical mental state reasoning to the practical resolution of user beliefs with objective reality.

  • •

    We introduce SynchToM, comprising four types of practical scenarios with interaction trajectories. It reveals a critical “ToM-Resolution Linkage”, where ground-truth mental states significantly boost task success, while misaligned modeling through shuffling causes systemic resolution failure.

  • •

    We validate a training paradigm using data generated by our pipeline to enhance the ToM capability and its practicality, highlighting the potential of ToM in assisting task-solving.

2 Related Works

2.1 Machine Theory of Mind

Theory of Mind (ToM) is literally defined as the cognitive capacity to attribute mental states to others, such as beliefs and intents, recognizing that these internal states may differ from their own and from objective reality (Premack & Woodruff, 1978; Apperly, 2010). It serves as the cornerstone of social cognition and interpersonal functions, including communication, empathy, pedagogical instruction, and conflict resolution (Jarvis et al., 2024). Early studies assessed the ToM capabilities of AI systems by adapting classical cognitive tests from psychology (Bubeck et al., 2023; van Duijn et al., 2023; Street, 2024), leading to the development of specialized benchmarks for evaluating ToM in LLMs, such as ToMBench (Chen et al., 2024), BigToM (Gandhi et al., 2023), FanToM (Kim et al., 2023), and Hi-ToM (Xu et al., 2024). Recent evaluations have expand into real-world interactive contexts (Xiao et al., 2025; Chan et al., 2024) and multimodal settings (Jin et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025).

Prior work has also explored various paradigms to enhance ToM reasoning in LLMs, including prompting strategies that explicitly expose models to perceptual discrepancies (Sclar et al., 2023; Wilf et al., 2024; Jung et al., 2024; Hou et al., 2024), model adaptation through supervised fine-tuning (Tang & Belle, 2024) and reinforcement learning (Lu et al., 2025), and Bayesian inverse planning to particularly model latent goals and beliefs of agents in complex multimodal settings (Jin et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2025). While these studies primarily assess or enhance ToM an isolated isolation capability, it remains under-explored of examining how ToM manifests and functions in real-world user-agent applications. We address this gap by grounding ToM in practical user-agent settings, which operationalizes ToM within interaction trajectories to improve user-centered outcomes.

2.2 User-Agent Interaction

Recent work has transitioned LLM agents from static instruction following to interactive, multi-step decision-making (Yao et al., 2024; Qian et al., 2025; Barres et al., 2025). A central challenge in these settings is handling under-specified or ambiguous user inputs, which is typically addressed through clarification strategies and implicit preference inference (Vijayvargiya et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025; Zhou et al., 2025). While these approaches usually excel at user profile modeling, they generally assume that user intent is well-defined and can be recovered through interactions, treating user expressions as incomplete yet reliable signals. However, these overlook the fact that users may hold subjective or erroneous beliefs about the environment. In contrast, our work frames user-agent interaction as a belief calibration problem, grounding ToM in interaction trajectories not only to infer and align with internal user beliefs but also resolve these conflicts.

3 Task Definition

To investigate the two research questions raised in Section 1, we formalize the framework through the lens of Bayesian Theory of Mind (Alanqary et al., 2021). We simulate interaction scenarios where the local observations of a user provide incomplete view of the environment (e.g., un unseen system configuration or a hidden error). The user should navigate through this partial observation to achieve a specific task, while an LLM agent moniters the interaction to provide feasible assistant. This section details our formulation following the three layers shown in Figure 1, the environment, the user beliefs, and the agent observations.

The environment.

The ground-truth environment is defined as a tuple ℰ=⟨𝒮,𝒜,𝒯,Ω,𝒪⟩\mathcal{E}=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{T},\Omega,\mathcal{O}\rangle, where 𝒮\mathcal{S} and 𝒜\mathcal{A} represent the state and action spaces, respectively. The transition dynamics are defined by 𝒯:𝒮×𝒜→𝒮\mathcal{T}\hskip-2.84544pt:\mathcal{S}\hskip-1.42271pt\times\hskip-1.42271pt\mathcal{A}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}, and 𝒪:𝒮→Ω\mathcal{O}:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\Omega maps states to observations. Let s∗∈𝒮s^{*}\in\mathcal{S} denote the true latent state of the environment (e.g., the underlying root cause of an error). The user cannot observe s∗s^{*} directly but perceives an observation ou∈Ωo^{u}\in\Omega (e.g., an error log) instead.

The user.

While the environment encompasses a vast state and observation space, the user operates under limited observability in practice. Unlike standard planners that optimize gold trajectories based on the true latent state s∗s^{*}, the user plans over a subjective and potentially flawed mental model (the partial observation in Figure 1). We formalize this partial view as the cognitive state Ψu\Psi_{u}.

Definition 3.1 (User Cognitive State).

The user cognitive state is defined as a tuple Ψu=⟨g,b⟩\Psi_{u}=\langle g,b\rangle, where:

  • •

    g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} is the declared intent, representing the explicit goal the user wants to achieve (e.g., “resolve the bug”).

  • •

    b∈Δ⁡(𝒮)b\in\Delta(\mathcal{S}) is the user latent belief distribution over the state space 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Constrained by user profile 𝒫\mathcal{P} (encapsulating limited perspective and specific domain knowledge), this belief may diverge from reality: b⁡(s∗)≪1b(s^{*})\ll 1 or DK​L(b||δs∗)>ϵD_{KL}(b||\delta_{s^{*}})>\epsilon, where δs∗\delta_{s^{*}} is the distribution of the true state.

Driven by the latent belief bb, the user produces its interaction trajectory τ={(at,ot)}t=1T\tau=\{(a_{t},o_{t})\}_{t=1}^{T} by maximizing an expected utility with respect to their belief. 𝔼s∼b​[⋅]\mathbb{E}_{s\sim b}[\cdot] denotes the expectation over latent state ss sampled from bb. Q⁡(s,at,g)Q(s,a_{t};g) represents the state-action value function, quantifying the expected cumulative utility of action ata_{t} in a subjective state towards the goal gg and hth_{t} is the interaction history:

πu​(at∣ht;g,b)∝exp⁡(𝔼s∼b​[Q⁡(s,at,g)]),\pi_{u}(a_{t}\mid h_{t};g,b)\propto\exp\left(\mathbb{E}_{s\sim b}\left[Q(s,a_{t};g)\right]\right),\vskip-3.0pt (1)

Consequently, the user interaction trajectory τ\tau is a realization of this subjective planning process:

τ∼P⁡(τ∣o,g,b)=∏t=1Tπu​(at∣ht−1,o,g,b).\tau\sim P(\tau\mid o,g,b)=\prod_{t=1}^{T}\pi_{u}(a_{t}\mid h_{t-1},o,g,b).\vskip-5.0pt (2)

This formulation captures the core problem: the user executes actions that are optimal for their (erroneous) belief bb, but potentially suboptimal for the true state s∗s^{*} and their interaction trajectory may deviate from the gold trajectory.

The agent.

Acting as a global monitor and our evaluation objective, the agent maintains a broader observational scope than the user. It has access to both (ou,g,τ)(o^{u},g,\tau) from user and world knowledge. However, the agent cannot directly access the user latent belief bb. Consequently, the the agent need to infer this belief bb through the given information (ou,g,τ)(o^{u},g,\tau). We formalize the model inference process as follows:

P⁡(b∣o,g,τ)=P⁡(τ∣o,g,b)⋅P⁡(b∣o,g)∫ℬP⁡(τ∣o,g,b′)​P​(b′∣o,g)​d​b′.P(b\mid o,g,\tau)=\frac{P(\tau\mid o,g,b)\cdot P(b\mid o,g)}{\int_{\mathcal{B}}P(\tau\mid o,g,b^{\prime})P(b^{\prime}\mid o,g)\,db^{\prime}}.\vskip-5.0pt (3)
  • •

    Likelihood P⁡(τ∣o,g,b)P(\tau\mid o,g,b): Measures how well belief bb explains user actions. If a user repeatedly checks a correct configuration, the model infers a belief bb where that configuration is suspect.

  • •

    Prior P⁡(b∣o,g)P(b\mid o,g): Represents common misconceptions associated with observation oo and goal gg.

The agent constructs an inferred belief b^\hat{b} by maximizing the posterior:

b^=arg​maxb∈ℬ⁡log⁡P⁡(τ∣o,g,b)⏟Action Consistency+log⁡P⁡(b∣o,g)⏟Prior Knowledge.\hat{b}=\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\underbrace{\log P(\tau\mid o,g,b)}_{\text{Action Consistency}}+\underbrace{\log P(b\mid o,g)}_{\text{Prior Knowledge}}.\vskip-3.0pt (4)

The agent obtains b^\hat{b}, traces back to derive the user profile 𝒫\mathcal{P} that induces this belief, and identifies the true latent state. These components constitute the three evaluation dimensions (b,𝒫,s∗)(b,\mathcal{P},s^{*}) in our experiment. This process allows the agent to synchronize its understanding with the user perspective, enabling it to rectify misconceptions rather than merely executing a potentially erroneous instruction gg.

The formulation above defines the ideal cognitive process of a ToM-capable agent. However, in practice, evaluating whether an LLM actually performs such Bayesian-like inference requires a controlled environment where the ground-truth latent belief bb, the true latent state s∗s^{*}, and the interaction trajectory τ\tau are explicitly known. To this end, we introduce SynchToM, a benchmark designed to operationalize this framework by synthesizing complex interaction scenarios that manifest these latent variables.

4 Assessing ToM in Practical Scenarios

To investigate the first research question (RQ1), “Can ToM be evaluated via its utility in practical scenarios rather than as an isolated cognitive task?”, we introduce a benchmark SynchToM. It evaluates ToM within complex interaction scenarios, specifically focusing on the agent ability to synchronize the user latent belief bb with the true state s∗s^{*} depicted in Figure 1, and infer the user profile and the root cause that drive such belief. Rather than relying static and theoretical ToM tasks, we synthesize user interaction trajectories by extending existing benchmark spanning four different practical scenarios, software engineering, user preference inference, education, and culture differences. This section introduces the construction of these scenario-grounded instances, provides dataset statistics, and presents the results and analysis of our evaluation.

4.1 Data Construction

As shown in Figure 2, we design a generation-and-validation pipeline to construct instances that evaluate ToM as a functional mechanism, instantiating the variables defined in Section 3. This pipeline contains a two-stage data generation procedure coupled with a validation module to ensure that the resulting data provides a high-fidelity signal for evaluating the Bayesian inference process.

In the first stage, the scenario synthesis stage, we curate a foundational portfolio of ToM scenarios by drawing from four domains: software engineering (SWE) (Chowdhury et al., 2024), preference modeling (PREFEVAL) (Zhao et al., 2025), culture split of MUCAR (Wang et al., 2025b), and education (The Pedagogy Benchmark) (Lelièvre et al., 2025). Each scenario comprises user latent beliefs bb, user profiles 𝒫\mathcal{P}, observations oo, explicit instructions gg, and the corresponding ground-truth latent states s∗s^{*}. While 𝒫\mathcal{P} and s∗s^{*} are derived directly from raw data to preserve factual grounding, bb, oo, and gg are synthesized via an LLM, conditioned on the original context to ensure epistemic consistency. This design creates the initial divergence between bb and s∗s^{*} that requires functional resolution. In the following trajectory construction stage, based on the generated scenarios, we simulate user behaviors via multi-turn interaction trajectories that reflect the evolution of their beliefs. For computational efficiency, we limit each trajectory by 10 turns. To ensure integrity of SynchToM, we introduce an LLM-based validation module to exam data across five dimensions, including behavioral faithfulness, realism, action consistency, inferability, and cognitive soundness. This module assigns scores ranging from 0 to 5, where instances scoring below 4 are subjected to iterative refinement and will be discarded after 5 iterations. This rigorous filtering ensures that our generated instances capture the practical reconciliation of beliefs within implicitly expressed interactions. Details of data curation are provided in Appendix A.

Statistics.

Our SynchToM benchmark comprises 390 high-fidelity test instances, each spanning a 10-turn interaction trajectory to ensure a sustained evaluation of belief reconciling. The quality of these instances is rigorously controlled by the validation module. SynchToM scores 4.41 on average out of 5.0, showing high behavioral faithfulness and cognitive consistency. Detailed scores for each validated dimensions are listed in Table 1. To facilitate model enhancement, we also construct an accompany training dataset of 6,522 trajectory-based instances, including 1,656 instances from SWE, 3,117 from The Pedagogy Benchmark, and 1,749 from PREFEVAL, providing the diverse supervision necessary for robust epistemic divergence detection.

4.2 Evaluation on Our Benchmark

Evaluation experiments are conducted across a diverse set of proprietary and open-source models. Proprietary models include GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025), Gemini 3 Pro (Google, 2025), Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025), and Grok 4 (xAI, 2025). And open-source models include Qwen3-32B and -8B (Yang et al., 2025a), Ministral-3 (Liu et al., 2026), DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025), MiniMax-M2.1 (MiniMax, 2025), and Kimi-K2-Thinking (Bai et al., 2025).

Model Inference.

To conduct evaluation with our benchmark, we provide models with the inputs specified “Inference Inputs during Evaluation” in Figure 2, and prompt models to generate outputs corresponding to the fields marked by “Evaluation Target of Our Benchmark” in Figure 2. following Equation 3 and 4. For the trajectory, we implement a step-wise evaluation by varying the number of revealed interaction turn. This allows us to measure the ToM reasoning efficiency of each models. Practically, models correctly infer bb, 𝒫\mathcal{P} and final solutions within fewer turns are believed to possess a more robust ToM capability. This evaluation design ensures that the benchmark measures not only the final result, but the efficiency and accuracy of the underlying epistemic reconciling process. To maintain ecological validity and align with the unpredictable nature of real-world interactions, our evaluation follows a zero-shot setting. Detailed evaluation prompts are provided in Appendix B.3.

LLM-based Scoring.

We employ the LLM-as-a-Judge framework (Zheng et al., 2023) for automated evaluation, and design three evaluation dimension for assessing both the cognitive depth and the functional utility of ToM:

  • •

    Latent Belief Explanation (Belief): It measures whether models precisely understand the gap and identify the cause of divergence between s∗s^{*} and bb, reflecting the core ToM ability of models.

  • •

    User Profile Modeling (Profile): It measures the ability to maintain a consistent user persona, including tone, preferred viewpoint, and behavioral bias. These usually shape the preference and habit, which are correlated with user intent and are critical for predicting the desired outcome.

  • •

    Problem Resolution (Solution): This measures the final accuracy and the logical viability of the predicted answer. We hypothesis that precise prediction of bb and 𝒫\mathcal{P} a prerequisite for identifying the true underlying need and providing a successful resolution.

To maintain computational efficiency, we utilize Qwen3-32B as our primary automated LLM judger, and we also discuss the plausibility and reliability of this model across different LLMs as judgers in Section 4.2. To build more feasible criteria, we exploit LLM-generated instance-specific rubrics (Hashemi et al., 2024) that extend the above evaluation dimension into elaborate checklists. Please refer to Appendix B for evaluation details.

Reliability Analysis of Scoring Mechanism

To establish the validity of our employed LLM judger, we conduct a meta-evaluation comparing Qwen3-32B against high-capacity models such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Pro. Scoring results are listed in Table 2, where Qwen3-32B achieves substantial inter-LLM agreement, particularly in the the Belief dimension that around 95% instances are scored similarly across LLMs. We provide the detailed confusion matrix across models in Appendix B.2

4.3 Benchmark Results

Table 3 provides a granular view of how LLMs scale across different reasoning intensities, including the vanilla setting without assistance of the trajectory, 5- and 10-turn settings. We report the results of three evaluation dimension, Latent Belief, Profile, , and Solution, across four practical scenarios. Surprisingly, we notice that proprietary models do not always present leading performance. Smaller open-source models, such as Kimi-K2, MiniMax-M2.1, achieve slightly better overall performance than Claude-Sonnet-4.5. This suggests that the functional application of ToM is a distinct capability from general instruction following and reasoning.

Domain Sensitivity: ToM utility is highly dependent on the underlying world knowledge of LLMs.

We observe distinct model behaviors across different scenarios, with most models score higher in SWE and Culture compared to Preference and Education. This performance gap potentially stems from the fact that current models acquire better knowledge about software engineering and culture nuances, enabling better detection of epistemic gaps between user subjective beliefs and true environment states for these scenarios, while struggling to develop accurate understanding for more complicate, variable, and subjective settings such as user preference modeling and educational scenarios.

Dimension Decoupling: Latent belief tracking remains the bottleneck for functional problem resolution.

The Belief score tends to be more stubborn comparing to the other two evaluation dimensions. While it increases with reasoning, the growth is shallower than the Solution dimension. This indicates that while reasoning navigates a model to predict better answers, it does not overwrite its internal inference of user mental states as easily. This decoupling highlights that correctly resolving tasks does not guarantee an accurate understanding of the user latent beliefs, further justifying our multi-dimensional evaluation of ToM.

4.4 Ablation Study

The main results establish a performance landscape across models, we continue to develop a deeper understanding of the ToM factors and their functional utilities with our benchmark. We conduct a series of ablation studies designed to isolate the causal impact of ToM on problem resolution. By injecting ground-truth cognitive states and perturbing belief-profile alignment through input shuffling, we investigate the relationship between theoretical dimensions, beliefs and profiles, and the functional dimension, the solution. Our findings reveal that accurate epistemic alignment is a critical prerequisite for resolution, particularly in partially observable environments, providing empirical evidence that ToM can be a functional utility beyond an isolated cognitive trait.

ToM-Resolution Linkage: Ground-truth ToM factors significantly boost task success in information-sparse environments.

To further investigate the role of functional ToM in LLMs, we conducted an ablation study by providing the models (Gemini-3-Pro, MiniMax-M2.1, Qwen3-8B) with either ground-truth user belief or profile, supplying both, and random shuffling. The trends of this ablation study are shown in Figure 3, while injecting both golden belief and profile yields the highest overall gains, investigated models present diverse sensitivity to individual belief and profile. For instance, MiniMax-M2.1 benefits more from solely golden profile than belief, while Gemini-3-Pro presents the highest gain with golden belief alone.

Causal Verification: Misaligned mental state modeling leads to significant resolution failure.

To examine whether theoretical ToM dimensions, user latent belief and profile, exhibit causal relationships with the task success, we perturb belief-profile signal by shuffling the original user belief and profile information and randomly reassign them to different instances, thereby breaking their alignment with the interaction trajectory. As shown by the red bars in Figure 3, all models experience performance degradation when the alignment between the mental model and the interaction is broken, indicating that accurate belief-reality synchronization plays a causal role in effective problem resolution. Detailed results of providing either and both ground-truth belief and profile information are provided in Appendix C.2.

Trajectory Improved Robustness: Interaction context is essential for the stabilization of belief reconciliation.

For in-depth analysis of the influence of interaction trajectories, we conduct turn-wise ablation studies varying the number of interaction turns on MiniMax-M2.1 (see Figure 4 and Appendix C.1 for the resulting trend and detailed results). We observe that while models achieve occasional success in early turns, stable epistemic reconciliation requires sustained interaction, particularly in Preference and Education domains, where nuanced latent states demand more evidence for disambiguation.

Our experiments further show that dense trajectories enhance model resilience: as interaction turns increase, models become more epistemically grounded, showing reduced reliance on explicit “golden” ToM signals and higher resistance to perturbed priors.

4.5 Case Study

We present a representative case from the Culture scenario to illustrate the divergence in ToM reasoning across models (see Appendix E for full detailed case).

In this scenario, a Western home cook attempts to prepare Chinese hot pot by dissolving sesame paste (zhima jiang) directly into boiling water, mistakenly treating it as a bouillon-like concentrate. Shaped by prior experience with instant miso or curry paste, the user interprets the failure of the paste to dissolve as a mechanical problem requiring more heat or stirring, rather than recognizing the fundamental incompatibility between the hydrophobic paste and water.

The two models exhibit distinct reasoning strategies. InternLM frames the problem as a physics optimization task: it correctly identifies the lack of emulsifying properties but proposes adding egg yolks or cornstarch to force dissolution, which is a technically grounded yet culturally incongruous solution that accepts the flawed premise of user. In contrast, GPT-5 identifies the deeper cognitive misalignment: the user has miscategorized the functional role of ingredient entirely. Rather than optimizing the flawed procedure, GPT-5 performs explicit premise correction (“This paste is a dipping sauce, not a soup stock”) and redirects the user toward culturally authentic alternatives.

This contrast highlights a critical dimension of ToM: lower-performing models optimize within the stated frame of user, whereas higher-performing models recognize when latent beliefs are fundamentally incorrect and intervene at the epistemic level.

5 Functional Enhancement via ToM-Scenarios

Evaluation results indicate that interaction trajectories provide evidence for belief reconciliation, where extended context enables agents to shift from intermittent guesses to stable epistemic alignment. Addressing RQ2, “How can ToM-based reasoning be integrated to improve downstream task performance?” (in Section 1), we propose two approaches using our curated scenario data: a trajectory-grounded reinforcement learning paradigm and a training-free multi-agent collaboration framework, to improve functional ToM.

5.1 Reinforcement Learning with Trajectory Data

To further improve ToM capability and its applicability in practical scenarios, we implement Reinforcement Learning (RL) via GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with our generated dataset. We insert ToM-specific tokens, “<ToM_Belief>...</ToM_Belief>” and “<ToM_Profile>...</ToM_Profile>”, for guiding the models to focus on the cognitive gap between user belief and the true state. The corresponding format reward denoted as rf​o​r​m​a​tr_{format}. We design a ToM reward according to the evaluation dimension of SynchToM, including rbr_{b}, rpr_{p}, and rs​o​lr_{sol}. The final reward computes as:

r=λf​o​r​m​a​t​rf​o​r​m​a​t+λb​rb+λp​rp+λs​o​l​rs​o​l,r=\lambda_{format}r_{format}+\lambda_{b}r_{b}+\lambda_{p}r_{p}+\lambda_{sol}r_{sol}, (5)

where we set λf​o​r​m​a​t\lambda_{format}=0.1, λb\lambda_{b}=0.25, λp\lambda_{p}=0.25, and λs​o​l\lambda_{sol}=0.4 in our experiments. By training on a mixture of 10-turn trajectory data, the model learns to update its internal representation of the user following with respect to the scenario-oriented mental states.

Experimental settings.

We build our model with two-stage RL training to fully exploit our curated data. In the initial training stage, we utilized data with trajectory lengths randomly ranging from 3 to 10 turns to provide more flexibility and diversity. Observing that longer trajectories enhanced the stability of model performance, we further adjusted the second stage to focus on longer trajectories, typically between 8 to 10 turns.

Results and Robustness Analysis.

We evaluate the efficacy of this approach through both the functional ToM performance (Table 4) and a stability analysis of all evaluation dimensions across five independent runs (Figure 5).

As illustrated in the bottom row of Figure 5, our model achieves consistent improvements in the Solution dimension, particularly at trajectory lengths of 5 and 10 turns. This aligns with our objective of leveraging ToM for practical scenarios, which also demonstrates that functional ToM can be enhanced via detailed interaction trajectory that reveals the true need and profile of users. Notably, despite the absence of domain-specific training data for Culture, the model demonstrates strong generalization, outperforming the base model with manageable variance. While performance in some vanilla settings (without presenting trajectories) showed a slight decline, this is consistent with our findings in Section 4.4, where shorter trajectories exhibited higher variance.

In the Latent Belief dimension, the model maintains performance levels comparable to or exceeding the baseline. The gains are particularly notable and consistent in the Education and Culture domains, reinforcing the observation that the model effectively utilizes interaction history to refine its internal epistemic states rather than relying solely on static profiling. Furthermore, although profile modeling scores decrease in certain instances, the scores for latent belief explanation remain stable or increase. This echoes our findings in Figure 3, suggesting that Qwen-8B derives greater benefit from dynamic belief inference than from static profile modeling.

5.2 Training-free Multi-agent Collaboration

In addition to training-based approaches, we hypothesize that ToM performance can also be improved in training-free manners where ToM reasoning enhances broader task performance across models. We design a multi-agent framework for further investigation, which is detailed in Appendix D. For faster validation, we conduct experiment with three open-source models, InternLM3-8B, DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-8B. We choose Qwen3-8B to be the backbone generator to see if the mental states prediction can translate across models and further boost the resolution. For comparison with choosing both the optimal b∗b^{*} and 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}, we also conduct experiments that only vote for either b∗b^{*} or 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}.

Results are listed in Table 11 in Appendix D, showing that utilizing optimal belief and profile predictions from the multi-agent pool consistently improves Solution performance for Qwen3-8B, though the magnitude varies by scenario. Culture scenarios see the highest improvement (+11.97), suggesting cross-model transfer effectively resolves nuances missed by single models. Preference modeling shows steady gains (up to +2.57), reinforcing the role of accurate profiles in user satisfaction. Notably, SWE and Education performance recovers from a slight negative in vanilla settings to +1.58 and +1.44, respectively, with 10-turn trajectories, indicating that technical ToM requires extended context to stabilize. These findings confirm that ToM reasoning chains are transferable, serving as effective guidance across models in collaborative tasks.

6 Conclusion

In this paper, we investigate two research questions regarding the functional applicability of Theory of Mind (ToM) for LLMs in interactive scenarios. We introduced SynchToM to shift the evaluation of ToM from mental state diagnostics to functional task utility grounding to practical scenarios, addressing RQ1. Our findings establish a robust ToM-resolution linkage, demonstrating that accurate mental state attribution is a causal driver of task success, particularly in information-sparse environments where interaction history is limited. We show that while models exhibit occasional accuracy in early turns, sustained interaction is required for stable epistemic reconciliation. Regarding RQ2, we demonstrate that ToM capabilities are both transferable and trainable through the utilization of our curated ToM-scenario data. Our work indicates that functional ToM is a critical, measurable component for the development of more collaborative and resilient models and AI agents.

Appendix A Data Construction Details

A.1 Prompt Templates for Data generation

We present the prompt templates used for scenario and trajectory generation in Table 5. While the overall structural framework is consistent across tasks, the concrete narrative details are adapted to task-specific contexts.

The scenario generation prompt converts task-relevant inputs such as QA pairs and user preferences, into a Theory of Mind setting that explicitly involves a mismatch between the true latent state and the user latent belief. In addition to these variables, the prompt also generates the root cause of the misconception, a paraphrased user profile, an observation, and the explicit instruction from user.

The trajectory generation prompt then takes the outputs of the scenario generation stage as input and produces a 10-turn simulated interaction trajectory, consisting of sequential user actions and corresponding observations.

A.2 Data Validation

Criteria for data validation

To ensure the reliability and logical consistency of the generated dataset, we established a rigorous evaluation protocol based on five core dimensions. The data quality is assessed against the following criteria:

  1. C1.

    Latent Belief & User Profile Alignment: Evaluates whether the user’s hidden belief is consistent with their profile and if the profile can be reasonably inferred from the belief.

  2. C2.

    Latent Belief & True State Relationship: Checks if the belief and the true state are thematically related, if the gap between them represents a reasonable misconception, and if an objective solution exists.

  3. C3.

    Trajectory & Latent Belief Consistency: Determines if the user’s trajectory (actions and thoughts) uniquely implies the latent belief and if the actions are specific to that belief while maintaining rigor.

  4. C4.

    Trajectory & User Profile Consistency: Assesses if the actions reflect the user’s background knowledge and characteristics, allowing for the unique determination of the user profile.

  5. C5.

    Trajectory Realism: Ensures the trajectory complies with physical common sense and social norms, evaluating the logic and detail level of observations and actions.

We use GPT 5.2 in the validation process. If the score assigned by GPT is lower than 4, the generated data is discarded and regenerated.

Prompt Template for data validation

We utilize a dedicated prompt to automate or assist in this evaluation process. The prompt instructs the evaluator to score each dimension on a scale of 0 to 5 and provide specific reasoning. The detailed prompt template is shown in Table 6.

Appendix D Training-free Multi-agent Collaboration

To validate that improved ToM reasoning can enhance broader task performance across models, we conduct experiments using a multi-agent framework. We denote the backbone generator LLM as ℳg​e​n\mathcal{M}_{gen} and treat the inference of latent states as a collaborative selection process. Formally, given a set of candidate models 𝒞={m1,m2,…,mn}\mathcal{C}=\{m_{1},m_{2},...,m_{n}\}, each model mim_{i} generates a predicted belief bib^{i} and profile 𝒫i\mathcal{P}_{i}. We employ the same judger and rubrics as we employed throughout the evaluation. We denote judge model is denoted as 𝒥\mathcal{J} and the instance-specific rubrics as ℛ\mathcal{R} to assign quality scores:

si=𝒥⁡(b^i,𝒫^​i∣ℛ).s_{i}=\mathcal{J}(\hat{b}_{i},\hat{\mathcal{P}}i\mid\mathcal{R}). (6)

The optimal latent states (b∗,𝒫∗)(b^{*},\mathcal{P}^{*}) are selected via:

(b∗,𝒫∗)=arg⁡max⁡(b^i,𝒫^​i)​si.(b^{*},\mathcal{P}^{*})=\arg\max{(\hat{b}_{i},\hat{\mathcal{P}}i)}{s_{i}}.\vskip-6.0pt (7)

The final task resolution yy is then generated by the backbone conditioned on these optimized inputs:

y=ℳ​g​e​n​(y∣ht,g,b∗,𝒫∗).y=\mathcal{M}{gen}(y\mid h_{t},g,b^{*},\mathcal{P}^{*}).\vskip-6.0pt (8)

For faster validation, we conduct experiment with three open-source candidate models, InternLM3-8B, DeepSeek-R1 and Qwen3-8B. Qwen3-8B achieves a better overall performance among the three, and we choose it to be ℳg​e​n\mathcal{M}_{gen} to see if the mental states prediction can translate across models and further boost the resolution. For comparison with choosing both the optimal b∗b^{*} and 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}, we also conduct experiments that only vote for either b∗b^{*} or 𝒫∗\mathcal{P}^{*}.

Experimental Results.

As shown in Table 11, providing Qwen3-8B with optimal belief and profile, and either of the two predictions from the multi-agent pool leads overall gains in Solution performance, but the effect diverges across scenarios. The most notable improvement occurs in the Culture scenarios, with a substantial gain of +11.97 in both vanilla and 10-turn settings. This suggests that ToM mental states can be inferred from our curated scenario data, and can be translated across different models to help resolve complex cultural nuances that a single model might overlook. In Preference modeling, we observe consistent improvements (up to +2.57), supporting the idea that accurate profile modeling is a key driver of preference satisfaction. Interestingly, in SWE, the gains are slightly negative in the vanilla setting, possibly because the solution to software bugs are more context-dependent and requiring additional ToM modeling from more complete trajectories, while the 10-turn result of SWE when providing both optimal belief and profile from the agents pool still yields a gain of +1.58.

This experiment confirms that ToM reasoning chains are transferable across models, and a high-quality mental state inferred by one model can serve as an guidance for another to enable multi-agent collaboration for downstream tasks.

Appendix E Complete Case for Case Study

In this section, we provide a representative failure case from the Culture scenario involving the preparation of a traditional Chinese dish.

Original Scenario: The Hot Pot Misconception

The user, modeled as a Western home cook familiar with “instant” culinary cultures (e.g., miso soup or bouillon cubes), attempts to prepare a Chinese hot pot, provided with a jar of sesame paste (zhima jiang) and a pot of boiling water.

  • •

    Explicit Instruction: “Dissolve this paste into the large pot of boiling water to create the soup stock.”

  • •

    User Latent Belief: The user maps the sesame paste to a “flavor packet” schema, assuming that any culinary paste in a jar is a concentrated base designed for aqueous dissolution (primary base for the broth).

  • •

    True Latent State: Physically, pure sesame paste is hydrophobic and lacks the surfactants necessary to dissolve in water without high-shear mixing or emulsifiers. Culturally, it is strictly a dipping sauce (tare) and is never used as the primary broth base.

  • •

    Interaction Trajectory: [Initial Attempt]: In Turn 1–3, The user unsuccessfully applies heat and agitation to integrate the paste. [Heuristic Fix]: In Turn 6–7, Lacking an understanding of the chemistry of the paste, The user adds soy sauce to visually correct the watery appearance of the broth. [The Cognitive Trap]: In Turn 9, the user achieves a local success by creating a small-scale emulsion in a side bowl (the correct dipping texture). This misleading milestone reinforces the user’s flawed mental model, leading them to mistakenly believe the method is scalable. [Terminal Failure]: In Turn 10, The attempt to apply this local logic to the main pot leads to a total culinary failure.
